brief.situation: You maintain stage_order.py at Ridgefield Community College (fictional). It orders 840 graduates by honor (summa, magna, cum laude, none) and alphabetically within each honor. Last week a teammate swapped the second sort for a hand-written quicksort 'for speed'. Today's list has every honor group right, but names inside the groups out of order. The printer needs the list at 13:00. It is 12:10.
handover: The script sorts twice: by last name, then by honor.
The roster has 840 rows; either sort takes well under a second.

Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The deadline runs on the same clock.
Sending is final for this case. Afterwards you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

scoring.modelReasoning: Sorting by name and then by honor gives 'by honor, then by name' only if the second sort is stable: elements with equal keys keep their relative order. Python's built-in sorted() is stable; a typical quicksort partitions by swapping across the array and is not, so graduates with the same honor came out in arbitrary order. Use sorted() for the second pass (or one sort on the composite key), check every adjacent pair, and never rewrite records to fit a sort. At 840 rows the speed gain was never real.
